course_description:
This course challenges students to think about how justice is carried out in a diverse society. Awareness of inequality, power and colonial structures are fundamental to our understanding of crime and criminal justice. Students will be exposed to theoretical and conceptual frameworks for understanding diversity, and gain an understanding of how marginalisation, inequality, and colonisation shape criminal justice systems and outcomes.

This course examines how power and privilege operate within criminal justice contexts to create disadvantages across social identities including race, gender, class, ability, sexuality, citizenship status, and more. Students will explore how different aspects of social identity intersect to compound experiences of inequality and social injustice, drawing on a range of relevant theories and tools. Beyond critical analysis, the course engages students in envisioning more equitable futures, testing their creativity to explore and develop new approaches to addressing systemic injustices. This solutions-oriented and 'fugitive thinking' approach develops essential skills including creative and critical thinking, effective communication, and advocacy strategies that prepare students for careers in criminal justice, social services, social policy development, justice advocacy, and much more. By combining theoretical understanding with practical skill development, students graduate equipped to contribute meaningfully to criminal justice reform efforts in their future professional roles.

CRIM2099/7099 is taught on St Lucia campus, and involves weekly seminars delivered in person .

The course relies on Blackboard Ultraﾠto provide students with learning materials relevant to each week’s workshop. Students are strongly encouraged to familiarise themselves with the course Blackboard site before the first week, and to engage with the weekly learning materials before joining our weekly workshops.

How much time should you spend on this course?

Students are expected to spend at least 10 hours each week on this course. This time can be divided roughly into three contact hours (combining lectures, workshop activities and discussion in class), and sevenﾠnon-contact hours (spent reading,ﾠcritically reflecting on the course learning materials andﾠcompleting the assessment tasks).

course_aims: The centralﾠaims of the course are (1) toﾠintroduce students to theoretical and conceptual frameworks for critically engaging with different aspects of social identity -- such as race, gender, sexuality, disability, class, citizenship status -- and the intersections of these, (2) to foster an understanding ofﾠmarginalisation, inequality, and colonisation as they shape criminal justice systems and outcomes, andﾠ(3) to encourage critical reflection of criminal justice practices; (4) to develop the skills and creative thinking needed to imagine and design fairer justice futures.

learning_outcomes.description: Describe key features of theoretical and conceptual frameworks for understanding categories of diversity (e.g., race, gender), and the intersections of these
Source, review, and critically evaluate/apply research addressing the implications of marginalisation, inequality, and colonisation on criminal justice outcomes
Demonstrate enhanced skills of problem solving, critical thinking, and reflection in diverse contexts
Demonstrate strong communication skills across diverse modes and settings

assessment_details.title: Group - 'Fairer Justice Futures' short proposals
assessment_details.category: Paper/ Report/ Annotation, Participation/ Student contribution
assessment_details.other_conditions: Peer assessed. See the conditions definitions
assessment_details.task_description: Students will be asked to move from analysis to future thinking-oriented action in weeks 9, 10 and 11. In weeks 10 and 11 in particular, students will arrange into smaller groups to design 'fairer justice futures'. The focus topics for these weeks include: i) crime prevention, and ii) policing. Students will be required to imagine and design 'fairer justice futures' proposals in relation to each of these two topics across the two weeks of seminars (weeks 10, 11). Students will be encouraged to use their creativity and apply the concepts of 'fugitive' and 'utopic' thinking - covered in early weeks of the semester - when developing their proposals. To be eligible for the 10% pass/fail (non-graded) mark, students must do the following in each of the two weeks (10, 11): attend the seminar, during the allocated time in the seminar, work in a smaller group to develop a short proposal -- using the template provided on Blackboard -- that in some way addresses the social inequalities discussed in previous weeks to achieve a fairer justice future, as a group, upload their proposal to the provided class Padlet page by the end of the relevant seminar, and in each of the weeks (and by the end of each respective week), engage with at least two other groups' proposals displayed on the class Padlet by undertaking a peer-review - adding constructive comments/feedback on the class Padlet page. To complete this assignment and receive their mark, each student is required to individually upload evidence of their Padlet posts and comments/engagement for the two weeks (10, 11) in week 12, using the template provided on Blackboard . This evidence is required to be uploaded via the provided Turnitin link in the Assignment 2 folder on Blackboard. Students will not be graded on this assignment; if they individually submit evidence of having completed the above tasks, they will receive the 10% available for this assignment. If they do not successfully submit evidence of their completion of the above tasks in each of the two weeks (10,11), they will receive zero marks for this assignment. Students who have a reasonable excuse for being unable to attend one of the seminars in weeks 10 or 11 (when Assignment 2 activities will be completed) should let the Course Coordinator know ASAP by email, and seek an alternative arrangement. Students with SAPs may also require adjustments to this task; please also contact the Course Coordinator if this is you. AI Use: This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex. Whilst students may use AI technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which AI may provide limited support and guidance. A failure to reference AI use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct Policy. Students may be required to complete an AI usage declaration and submit it with their assessment. Additional resources are available through UQ AI Student Hub . assessment_details.title: Individual 'Fairer Justice Futures' long proposal
assessment_details.task_description: Individually, students will work with the ideas they gathered during Assignment 2 (group work) -- as well as feedback on Assignment 2 received from their peers -- to develop a fuller individual researched proposal for a fairer justice future. Their proposal must relate, broadly, to one of the topics covered in weeks 9-11: i) crime prevention, ii) policing, or ii) abolitionist/alternative futures. A proposal template for this final assignment will be provided via Blackboard. Students MUST use this template for their proposal submission. This assignment will be graded according to the rubric provided on Blackboard. Word count: Individual proposals are 2,000 words in length (+/- 10%) for CRIM2099 students; 2500 words in length (+/- 10%) for CRIM7099 students. The week 12 seminar will be dedicated to scaffolding students' successful completion of this final assignment. Students will then have weeks 13 and 14 to continue work on the assignment, before it is due at the beginning of week 15. AI Use: This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex.
